summary: The paper introduces the single-location regression (SLR) task in two variants (spiked-SLR and max-SLR) and uses tools from statistical physics / sequence multi-index models to compare softmax with linear (and other) attention. The main contributions are: (i) a proof that softmax attention attains the Bayes risk in the population limit while linear attention does not, with quantitative separation results in the strong-signal and long-sequence regimes; (ii) a replica-based characterization of the finite-sample test risk showing softmax still dominates. The setting is quite stylized (no query vectors, single relevant token, Gaussian tokens, manifold restriction) and the finite-sample result is non-rigorous, but the separation results are clean and directly address a well-motivated open question. Overall a solid, principled theoretical contribution near but slightly above the ICLR acceptance bar.
strengths: Tackles a well-motivated open question — the empirical dominance of softmax on retrieval tasks — with a principled, mathematically tractable model that is arguably the simplest setting where softmax and linear attention provably separate.

Clean population-level result: softmax is Bayes-optimal on both SLR variants under a natural condition on the weight function, whereas linear attention has explicit residual error that depends badly on sequence-length variance and on the max-SLR regime (Corollaries 4.3–4.4).
Corollary 4.1 gives a useful diagnostic (non-vanishing mean or asymmetry) explaining why bare linear or erf activations fail without a constant bias — a small but insightful design principle.
The comparison with softplus-normalized kernelized attention is instructive: it isolates 'normalization across tokens' vs. 'kernel growth rate' as two orthogonal ingredients of softmax's advantage.

The finite-sample replica calculation extends population-level insights into the proportional regime (α = N/D fixed), and numerical experiments with quasi-Newton optimization on finite N, D match the theoretical prediction quite well (Fig. 3), providing evidence that softmax's benefit is not just approximation-theoretic but also statistical/computational.

Related work is nuanced and honestly delineates concurrent contributions (Dohmatob 2025, Dragutinović et al. 2025, Barnfield et al. 2026), and clearly states how this work generalizes prior sequence multi-index setups (variable length, generic weighting, proper high-dimensional scaling).

key_concerns.issue: The core finite-sample characterization (Result 5.1) is derived by the non-rigorous replica method, and additionally simplified under a manifold/diagonal-order-parameter assumption that is not proved. The paper acknowledges this, but the main statistical-advantage claim in Section 5 rests on it. Without a proof (or at least stronger numerical validation across more regimes), the strength of this claim is closer to 'conjecturally' than 'we show'.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either (a) explicitly reframe Result 5.1 as a conjecture/heuristic prediction, and be explicit in the abstract/introduction that the finite-sample result is non-rigorous; or (b) provide stronger numerical validation of the manifold restriction (e.g., measuring the off-manifold order parameters mkv, mvk, qvk during training across seeds, L, ν, α) and of the replica prediction (multiple seeds, larger sweeps in α, and error bars).

key_concerns.issue: The manifold assumption M = {mkv = mvk = qvk = 0} is central both to population and finite-sample analyses, yet its justification is largely intuitive ('GD initialized on M stays on M', with a note that a formal proof is delicate and there exist other local minima off-manifold, per Appendix A.2.6). Since a substantive part of the paper's conclusions is 'softmax reaches Bayes / dominates linear on this manifold', a reader cannot be sure GD from random init converges to the on-manifold minimizer at finite D or under noise.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a systematic numerical study, at finite but growing D, showing (i) how far iterates drift from M during one-pass SGD and Adam, (ii) whether this depends on ν, L, α, and (iii) whether off-manifold local minima are ever encountered. If drift is nonzero, quantify the resulting excess risk vs. the on-manifold prediction.

key_concerns.issue: Empirical breadth is narrow. All experiments are on the synthetic SLR data model with L ≤ 10, one output channel, no query vector, Gaussian tokens, and a single quasi-Newton optimizer. The paper's motivation (Figure 1 replicated from Shen et al. 2024) is real LLM retrieval; the gap between the toy model and that motivating evidence is substantial, and no bridging experiment (e.g., a single-layer attention on a synthetic AR/MQAR task) is attempted. This weakens the significance claim.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add at least one experiment moving toward more realistic settings: e.g., a small trained attention layer on associative recall / MQAR (Arora et al. 2024) with softmax vs. linear vs. kernelized attention, and connect the observed separation to the population/finite-sample predictions here. Even a qualitative match would substantially raise the impact of the paper.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical soundness of the experiments is under-reported in the main text: number of seeds, confidence intervals, and variance for the quasi-Newton runs in Fig. 3 are not specified in the body (deferred to appendix). Given that the ERM problem is non-convex, seed-to-seed variation is a first-order concern for the claim that 'the softmax attention has lower error … across all tested hyperparameters'.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: In the main-text captions of Figs. 2 and 3, state the number of seeds, plot error bars/CIs, and comment on failure modes (e.g., how often the quasi-Newton optimizer got stuck in a bad local minimum) even if details go to the appendix.

key_concerns.issue: The paper claims (Section 4) that its population-risk analysis 'captures the performance efficiently attainable with one-pass SGD from random init', but this is asserted more than shown. In the high-D limit, the initial gradient on the recovery order parameters can be very small (Ben Arous et al. 2021 is cited), which typically induces sample-complexity thresholds; the paper does not quantify this for either activation, so 'efficiently attainable' is imprecise.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either compute (even heuristically) the sample/step complexity of one-pass SGD to escape the trivial fixed point for softmax vs. linear on SLR — this is the natural next step given Corollary 4.1 — or soften the wording ('this analysis is consistent with the fixed point of one-pass SGD' rather than 'captures efficiently attainable performance').

key_concerns.issue: Some clarity issues that would benefit a broader ICLR audience: (i) the introduction jumps from 'softmax dominates on retrieval' (Fig. 1) to 'we study single-location regression' without motivating why SLR is a good abstraction of retrieval, beyond the sentence 'akin to a toy in-context learning task'; (ii) notation is dense (7 vs. 4 vs. 6 order parameters across sections) and the mapping between population and finite-sample order parameters could be tabulated; (iii) the equations in Result 5.1 (17)–(25) are hard to parse because some subscripts (χ_ℓ, z_ℓ) and cases (ℓ = 1 vs. ℓ > 1) are introduced mid-formula.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a short paragraph 'Why SLR captures retrieval' at the end of Section 3.1, a table mapping the population order parameters to their finite-sample analogues in Result 5.1, and clean up the (17)–(25) block with explicit index conventions.

key_concerns.issue: The 'Bayes-optimal at finite α' curve in Fig. 3 is described as having a discontinuous 'hard phase' where first-order methods fail (Appendix B), but this is only mentioned in passing in the main text. Given how central the Bayes-optimal comparison is, the phenomenology deserves at least a short main-text discussion.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a short subsection or paragraph in Section 5 describing the hard phase qualitatively, and clarify whether the softmax ERM's gap to the Bayes-optimal risk in Fig. 3 is compatible with the standard statistical-to-algorithmic gap or reflects an intrinsic limitation of the softmax parameterization.

key_concerns.issue: The setting omits query vectors, positional encodings, multiple heads, and multi-layer stacking. This is acknowledged briefly ('a limitation of our setting'), but the limitations paragraph is very short and does not discuss which conclusions might change once these ingredients are added — especially since real retrieval circuits rely on induction heads that require at least two layers.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Expand the limitations discussion, in particular addressing (a) whether adding a learnable query would change the population-optimality result, (b) whether multi-head attention would help linear attention close the gap on max-SLR, and (c) how positional information interacts with the 'normalization matters' insight.

questions_for_authors: How sensitive is the manifold assumption to finite D? Concretely, if you initialize k, v randomly and run one-pass SGD (or Adam) on the empirical loss, how large are the off-manifold order parameters (mkv, mvk, qvk) at convergence relative to the on-manifold ones, as a function of D, L, ν?

Can you provide a numerical sanity check of Result 5.1 by comparing the replica prediction against ERM at multiple values of α, D, and multiple seeds, with error bars? A single-panel confirmation at √(ND) = 10⁴ is thin evidence for a non-rigorous claim.

In Corollary 4.3, cL is described as 'a constant that depends on L' — can you give its scaling with L? A linear or logarithmic dependence would materially change the interpretation of the softmax advantage as L grows.

Does the softmax's Bayes-optimality (Proposition 4.2) rely essentially on gν satisfying the multiplicative structure (6), and if so, are there natural retrieval-like tasks where this structure fails? A negative example would sharpen the scope of the claim.

For the max-SLR at finite ν (not the ν → ∞ limit reported in Corollary 4.3), how does the linear-vs-softmax gap behave? The current Corollary 4.3 gives asymptotic separation; a finite-ν version would connect more directly to realistic softmax temperature scaling.

Have you tried a small experiment on MQAR (Arora et al. 2024) with softmax vs. linear vs. softplus-normalized attention, to check whether the population-level intuitions here (normalization + fast-growing kernel) qualitatively predict which architectures succeed?

The added constant '1' in linear and erf activations breaks symmetry at initialization but is often absent in the theoretical linear-attention literature. Does your dominance result over linear attention still hold if the reader uses the pure identity σ(χ) = χ (which is what most prior theory studies), or is the constant an artifact of your parameterization?
In Fig. 3 the softmax's gap to the Bayes-optimal risk narrows as α grows — can you quantify the rate at which it closes (e.g., 1/α, 1/√α)?
calibration_check: Claims are mostly well scoped — 'softmax reaches the Bayes risk in the population limit under condition (6)' is precise, and the finite-sample statement is honestly flagged as replica-based. The wording that the population analysis 'captures the performance efficiently attainable by one-pass SGD' is somewhat over-scoped given the absence of an explicit sample-complexity result.

significance.justification: Directly addresses a live open question — why softmax dominates linear/kernelized attention on retrieval — with clean, quotable separation results. Impact is somewhat limited by the toy nature of the model and the absence of any bridge to realistic tasks.

novelty.justification: Builds heavily on existing sequence multi-index / spiked-token machinery (Marion et al. 2025, Cui 2025, Troiani et al. 2025); the main new ingredients are variable-length sequences, generic weighting gν, and the explicit softmax vs. linear separation. Concurrent works (Dohmatob 2025, Dragutinović et al. 2025) study closely related questions.

rigor.justification: Population-level Propositions 4.1–4.4 and Corollaries 4.1–4.4 appear rigorous. However, Result 5.1 is derived non-rigorously via replicas, and the manifold restriction is justified intuitively rather than proved — both are load-bearing for the main statistical-advantage claim.

statistical_soundness.justification: Experiments in Figs. 2–3 report the theoretical prediction and a single ERM run at √(ND) = 10⁴. Seed counts, error bars, variance across initializations, and the robustness of the quasi-Newton optimizer are not clearly reported in the main text, which is a real gap for a non-convex objective.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations of the manifold assumption, the non-rigorous replica method, and the missing query vector are all stated in the body, and concurrent works are cited fairly. A couple of phrases (e.g., 'efficiently attainable by one-pass SGD') slightly overreach relative to the evidence.

clarity.justification: The math is generally readable but dense; notation switches between 7-, 4-, and 6-dimensional order-parameter sets across sections, and the (17)–(25) block for Result 5.1 is hard to parse. The retrieval-to-SLR motivation is asserted rather than developed.

structure_compliance.justification: Follows a standard theory-paper structure (intro / related work / model / population analysis / finite-sample analysis) and stays within a reasonable ICLR length. Extensive appendices are appropriately referenced.

reproducibility.justification: The data model, activations, loss, and optimization procedure are described in detail; the replica fixed-point iteration is written out; regularization is tuned by grid search with details deferred to Appendix D. A dedicated code artifact is mentioned. Anonymized URL removal is not a factor per the review guidelines.

related_work.justification: Prior theoretical work on linear attention, sequence multi-index models, retrieval benchmarks (NIAH, AR, MQAR), and concurrent works on softmax advantages are all discussed and carefully positioned. The delineation of what is new relative to Cui (2025), Troiani et al. (2025), Marion et al. (2025), Dohmatob (2025), and Dragutinović et al. (2025) is clear.

figure_quality.justification: Judged from captions: Fig. 1 (reproduced motivation) frames the question well; Fig. 2 (population risk vs. ν for four activations, two tasks, three L regimes) directly supports the normalization-and-tail argument; Fig. 3 (finite-α theory vs. ERM) is the load-bearing empirical panel and is informative, though could benefit from error bars and more α values in the main text.

breadth_generality.justification: All experiments live in the synthetic SLR world with L ≤ 10, no query vectors, no positional encodings, and a single optimizer. The generality claim about 'softmax's advantage in retrieval' is only supported within this stylized model; no bridging experiment (e.g., MQAR, small trained attention on a semi-realistic sequence task) is provided.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline accept: a mathematically clean and well-motivated theoretical contribution with clear separation results, weakened by the non-rigorous finite-sample result, the unproven manifold assumption, and narrow empirical breadth. Consistent with a Minor-Revision grade at ICLR.
